title: Ogham
otherNames: Old Irish ogam, Modern Irish ogham
the feda (letters; singular fid, "wood, tree, letter")
family: Insular epigraphic alphabet of stroke-letters cut along a stemline. It was devised for Primitive Irish, almost certainly by someone who knew the Latin alphabet and Latin grammatical teaching. It is not derived from Hebrew, and it is not one of Agrippa's alphabets. The later medieval tradition elaborated it into a learned and cryptic ("secret") art.
summary: Ogham writes twenty letters (feda) as groups of one to five strokes set against a stemline. In four groups (aicmi) of five, the strokes fall on one side, on the other, across the line, or as notches on it. Later the manuscript tradition added five supplementary letters (forfeda). It is first found on some 400 memorial stones, mostly in southern Ireland, conventionally dated to the 5th-6th centuries (some argue for the 4th). Its key and its lore come from much later manuscripts: the Auraicept na nÉces, and In Lebor Ogaim (the "Ogam Tract") in the Book of Ballymote (c. 1390), which lists nearly a hundred cryptic "oghams". The doctrine that every letter is a tree is medieval scholarship. The tree calendar is Robert Graves's (The White Goddess, 1948).

firstAttestation.work: Orthodox ogham memorial inscriptions on standing stones (Macalister, CIIC I, 1945; McManus 1991; Ogham in 3D corpus)
firstAttestation.author: anonymous
firstAttestation.date: conventionally 5th-6th century AD; several scholars allow that the script was devised in the 4th century or earlier. No stone is dated: dating is by the language (Primitive Irish), the formulae, and comparison with the Latin-inscribed stones of Britain.
firstAttestation.place: southern Ireland, densest in Co. Kerry, Cork and Waterford; Irish settlements in south-west Wales (often bilingual with Latin), Devon and Cornwall, the Isle of Man and western Scotland; one stone from Silchester (Hampshire)
firstAttestation.locator: CIIC (Macalister 1945, 1949) numbers by county; Ogham in 3D (DIAS) site entries. No single locator: it is a corpus.
firstAttestation.notes: Rough counts: about 400 orthodox stones, the large majority in Ireland and about 40 in Wales [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]. Typical formula: X MAQI Y, "(the stone) of X son of Y", with names in the genitive. Other formula words are MUCOI "of the kin-group", AVI "of the descendant", ANM "name", KOI "here" and CELI "of the client/follower". The KEY to names and values is first attested much later, in manuscripts. The Auraicept na nÉces has a canonical core that Ahlqvist (1983) dates to the 7th century; its surviving copies are 14th-century and later. In Lebor Ogaim survives in the Book of Ballymote (Royal Irish Academy MS 23 P 12, c. 1390) and other late medieval manuscripts.

transmission.work: Orthodox stone inscriptions
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Uses the 20 letters (with rare traces of a supplementary X-sign) to carve personal names and lineage formulae, mostly as memorials and possibly as boundary/title markers.

transmission.work: Bilingual Latin-ogham stones in Wales and south-west Britain
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Pairs ogham with Latin capitals, e.g. Castell Dwyran (Carmarthenshire): Latin MEMORIA VOTEPORIGIS PROTICTORIS, ogham VOTECORIGAS [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]. The pairs later confirmed the values given by the manuscript key.

transmission.date: 7th c. (canonical core; Ahlqvist 1983) with later commentary layers
transmission.work: Auraicept na nÉces ("The Scholars' Primer")
transmission.author: anonymous; the tradition attributes the core to Cenn Fáelad (d. 679), an attribution to be reported as such
transmission.what: A treatise on Irish grammar. It sets ogham beside the Latin alphabet, names the four aicmi and the stroke positions relative to the stemline (druim), and holds that the letter names come from the names of Fénius Farsaid's best students or from trees.

transmission.work: "Scholastic" ogham inscriptions
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Inscriptions written in manuscript-period spelling, some using forfeda, cut by people who had learned ogham from the books rather than from living epigraphic practice.

transmission.work: Pictish and Norse-period oghams in Scotland (Forsyth 1996)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Ogham adopted beyond Irish-speaking areas, often with texts that are not readily interpretable (Brandsbutt, Lunnasting, Newton stones) [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].

transmission.work: Sanas Cormaic (Cormac's Glossary)
transmission.author: attributed to Cormac mac Cuilennáin (d. 908)
transmission.what: Glosses fé as an aspen rod inscribed with ogham, used to measure corpses and graves and dreaded to handle [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].

transmission.work: Ulster-cycle and other sagas (Táin Bó Cúailnge; Tochmarc Étaíne), Lebor na hUidre and Yellow Book of Lecan
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Literary ogham: Cú Chulainn's ogham on a withe and on a forked branch as challenges to an army; the druid Dalán's four yew rods inscribed with ogham used to find Étaín. Evidence for how medieval authors imagined ogham, not for pagan practice.

transmission.work: Book of Ballymote (RIA MS 23 P 12): Auraicept na nÉces and In Lebor Ogaim
transmission.author: compiled for Tomaltach Mac Donnchaidh; scribes include Solam Ó Droma, Robertus Mac Sithigh and Maghnus Ó Duibhgeannáin [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]
transmission.what: The fullest medieval treatment. It has the alphabet with names and tree glosses; the three Bríatharogam (word-oghams of Morann, Mac ind Óc and Cú Chulainn); about a hundred named "oghams" (bird, colour, crafts, hand and nose oghams and many others); and circular diagrams such as Fege Find.

transmission.work: Ogygia, seu rerum Hibernicarum chronologia (London)
transmission.author: Roderick O'Flaherty
transmission.what: Prints the alphabet in a "Beth-Luis-Nion" order with N third (B L N F S ...), against the order of the Auraicept and In Lebor Ogaim (B L F S N). Graves later took this order up.

transmission.work: The Mount Callan (Co. Clare) "ogham"
transmission.author: reported by Theophilus O'Flanagan
transmission.what: Antiquarian controversy: an inscription claimed as ancient and widely regarded as a forgery [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].

transmission.work: Auraicept na n-Éces: The Scholars' Primer (Edinburgh: John Grant)
transmission.author: George Calder (ed. and trans.)
transmission.what: Edition and English translation of the Auraicept and of the Ogam Tract from the Book of Ballymote and the Yellow Book of Lecan. It is the standard source for the "secret" oghams in English.

transmission.work: The Secret Languages of Ireland (Cambridge University Press)
transmission.author: R. A. S. Macalister
transmission.what: Argues that ogham began as a druidic finger-signing code (from a Greek alphabet). Influential on popular writing; not accepted by later scholarship.

transmission.work: Corpus Inscriptionum Insularum Celticarum, 2 vols (Dublin: Stationery Office)
transmission.author: R. A. S. Macalister
transmission.what: The standard numbered corpus (CIIC) of the stones.

transmission.work: The White Goddess: A Historical Grammar of Poetic Myth (London: Faber and Faber; revised later editions)
transmission.author: Robert Graves
transmission.what: Recasts O'Flaherty's Beth-Luis-Nion as a druidic tree-alphabet and 13-month tree calendar tied to a goddess cult. This is the source of the modern "Celtic tree calendar".

transmission.work: "The invention of the Ogom cipher", Ériu 26
transmission.author: James Carney
transmission.what: Argues that ogham was devised as a cipher-like script modelled on Latin.

transmission.work: The Early Irish Linguist (Helsinki: Societas Scientiarum Fennica)
transmission.author: Anders Ahlqvist
transmission.what: Edition of the canonical part of the Auraicept, with its dating.

transmission.work: "Irish letter-names and their kennings", Ériu 39; A Guide to Ogam (Maynooth Monographs 4)
transmission.author: Damian McManus
transmission.what: The standard modern account. Only some letter names are tree names, the kennings preserve non-tree meanings, and the forfeda are later additions; it also gives the origin debate and the corpus.

transmission.work: The Celtic Tree Oracle
transmission.author: Liz and Colin Murray
transmission.what: A modern divination system on Graves's tree-letters. It is one of several living practices to be reported, neither mocked nor endorsed [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].

transmission.work: Unicode 3.0, Ogham block U+1680-U+169F
transmission.author: Unicode Consortium (proposal associated with Michael Everson and Irish Standard I.S. 434:1999)
transmission.what: Encodes the 20 letters, 5 forfeda, peith, space mark and feather marks (29 characters; U+169D-169F unassigned, checked in this session).

claims.claim: Ogma mac Elathan invented ogham, devising it for the learned apart from rustics and herdsmen.
claims.evidence: Origin story told in In Lebor Ogaim / the Auraicept tradition. It is a medieval learned myth, reported as such.

claims.claim: The first thing written in ogham was seven b's on a birch rod, a warning to Lug mac Ethlenn; that is why b stands first.
claims.evidence: Same tract. An aetiological tale for the letter order [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].

claims.claim: The letter names were taken from the names of the 25 best scholars in the school of Fénius Farsaid (after Babel), or from trees.
claims.evidence: Auraicept na nÉces gives both explanations, inside its account of Fénius forming Irish from the languages of Babel.

claims.claim: Every ogham letter is named after a tree.
claims.evidence: The medieval tracts assign a tree to every letter. That is documented as medieval doctrine. But several names are ordinary words: úath "fear", tinne "ingot", gort "field", straif "sulphur", úr "earth". McManus shows the Bríatharogam kennings often point to these non-tree senses (e.g. kennings of tinne about weapons and metal). Only beithe, fern, sail, dair and coll are secure tree names, with ailm and onn possible.

claims.claim: Ogham was created in the 4th century or later by someone schooled in Latin grammar.
claims.evidence: Majority scholarly view. The arrangement into vowels and consonant classes and the letter inventory reflect Latin grammatical analysis, and the language of the stones is Primitive Irish. Alternatives: a cipher (Carney 1975); runic inspiration (older, minority); a druidic finger code from a Greek alphabet (Macalister 1937; abandoned). The date and place (Ireland, or Irish settlers in Roman Britain) remain open.

claims.claim: Ogham was a secret script of the druids.
claims.evidence: The stones are public memorials with plain formulae, not secrets. "Secret" applies to the medieval learned tradition: ogham as part of the poets' and grammarians' curriculum, the saga motif of messages only the learned can read, and the cryptic varieties in In Lebor Ogaim. No source contemporary with pagan druids describes ogham.

claims.claim: The c. 100 "secret" oghams of In Lebor Ogaim were used in real communication.
claims.evidence: They are documented as lists. Most are acrostics (each letter replaced by a word from one class: birds, colours, crafts, kings, rivers...) or graphic variants. Scholars generally treat them as scholastic exercises and mnemonics. Their actual use in messages is unattested outside literature.

claims.claim: Hand ogham (cos-ogam "shin ogham", srón-ogam "nose ogham") was a working sign language.
claims.evidence: The tract describes fingers laid against the shin or the ridge of the nose as stemline. That it was practised, rather than described, is not shown.

claims.claim: Druids divined with ogham-inscribed yew rods.
claims.evidence: Tochmarc Étaíne has the druid Dalán use four yew rods inscribed with ogham to discover where Étaín is. The tale is preserved in c. 1100 and later manuscripts. It is literary evidence only.

claims.claim: Ogham stones also served as markers of land ownership.
claims.evidence: Argued from Old Irish legal references to ogham in stone as evidence of title, and from the siting of stones [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].

claims.claim: The word "ogam" derives from the god Ogma (cf. Gaulish Ogmios in Lucian).
claims.evidence: The etymology is uncertain. Proposals include a link with Ogma/Ogmios and with Greek ógmos "furrow, line" (discussed by McManus). Lucian's Ogmios is a Gaulish Heracles figure of eloquence, and the link to the Irish Ogma is speculative.

claims.claim: The 13-month Celtic tree calendar (Birch, Rowan, Ash, Alder, Willow, Hawthorn, Oak, Holly, Hazel, Vine, Ivy, Reed, Elder) is an ancient druidic calendar.
claims.evidence: Graves presents it so in The White Goddess (1948), building on O'Flaherty's 1685 Beth-Luis-Nion order. No medieval Irish source contains a tree calendar. Historians treat it as Graves's poetic construction.

claims.claim: The Beth-Luis-Nion order (N third) is the ancient order.
claims.evidence: The Auraicept and In Lebor Ogaim have B L F S N. The stones carry texts, not alphabet rows, so they do not decide the order. N third is O'Flaherty's (1685) arrangement, followed by Graves.

claims.claim: Charles Graves, Bishop of Limerick and a 19th-century ogham scholar, was Robert Graves's grandfather.
claims.evidence: Family relationship well established in biographies of Robert Graves [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].

claims.claim: Unicode encodes Ogham at U+1680-U+169C; U+1680 is a (visible) space character.
claims.evidence: Checked mechanically in this session against the Unicode Character Database 14.0 (Python unicodedata) and Node's String.prototype.trim().

claims.claim: Ogham is one of the magical alphabets of Agrippa or the Renaissance grimoires.
claims.evidence: No such use is known to this researcher. Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (1533) gives Hebrew-based alphabets (Celestial, Malachim, Transitus Fluvii) and Theban, not ogham. Ogham belongs in the wing as a learned and cryptic script with its own tradition [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].

letters.name: beithe
letters.form: One straight stroke hanging perpendicular BELOW the horizontal stemline (to the RIGHT of a vertical stemline read upward). Each stroke touches the line and stops there; none crosses it. Each stroke is about 11 stemline-thicknesses long (381 units) and about twice as thick as the line (73 vs 33 units). Glyph advance 301 units.
letters.note: Name spellings vary: Old Irish (as given), Modern Irish and the Unicode name (BEITH) differ. nameMeaning follows McManus 1988/1991 as remembered. medievalTreeGloss is the tree that the medieval tracts assign. gravesTree is the tree of The White Goddess (1948). These are three different layers; do not merge them. [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]

letters.name: muin
letters.form: One long straight stroke CROSSING the stemline obliquely, each cut through at its midpoint. In the font each stroke slants from lower left to upper right (like '/'), leaning about 200 units over its 795-unit height (about 14 degrees off the vertical). It reaches as far below the line as a B-stroke and as far above as an H-stroke. The slant direction varies on stones and in manuscripts; the axis of the group is 'across', not the angle.

letters.name: ailm
letters.form: One small lozenge (diamond bead) threaded ON the stemline. Each lozenge is 147 units wide and 176 tall, with its horizontal diagonal lying along the line, so it rises 72 units above the line and drops 71 below it. This is the font's normalisation. On the stones the vowels are notches cut into the arris (the edge that serves as stemline). Many manuscript keys and modern charts draw them instead as short perpendicular strokes crossing the line.

letters.name: onn
letters.form: Two small lozenges (diamond beads) threaded ON the stemline. Each lozenge is 147 units wide and 176 tall, with its horizontal diagonal lying along the line, so it rises 72 units above the line and drops 71 below it. The beads are evenly spaced at the same 144-unit pitch as the strokes. This is the font's normalisation. On the stones the vowels are notches cut into the arris (the edge that serves as stemline). Many manuscript keys and modern charts draw them instead as short perpendicular strokes crossing the line.

letters.name: ébad
letters.form: An X: two straight strokes crossing each other ON the stemline, each running the full height (as far below as a B-stroke and as far above as an H-stroke; 795 units). The arms are symmetrical, and the crossing point sits on the line. Overall width 287 units, the same advance as a one-stroke letter.
letters.note: First of the five forfeda ('extra letters'). An X-shaped sign does occur on some orthodox stones. McManus (1991) discusses its use there for a /k/ sound, conventionally transliterated K [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]. The manuscript tradition gives it the value ea.
letters.stoneValue: X-sign, transliterated K on some stones (see note)
letters.medievalTreeGloss: glosses vary (aspen and elecampane are both given in modern summaries) [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]

letters.name: óir
letters.form: An outlined lozenge (diamond), centred on the stemline and taller than wide (795 x about 417 units). Its top point is level with the top of an H-stroke and its bottom point with the foot of a B-stroke. Its two side points lie on the line. The stemline runs straight through it along the horizontal diagonal, splitting the open interior into two triangles. The sides are straight strokes of normal thickness, and there are no other interior lines.
letters.note: The name is usually explained as the genitive of ór 'gold'. Manuscript drawings of this sign vary and were not checked in this session.
letters.stoneValue: not a regular letter of the orthodox stones [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]
letters.medievalTreeGloss: feorus, spindle-tree [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]

letters.name: uilen (uilleann)
letters.form: BELOW the line, a squared hook or spiral built from straight bars meeting at right angles. (1) A perpendicular downstroke hangs from the line exactly like a B-stroke, at x 114-187. (2) At its foot it turns right into a bottom bar running about 2.5 stroke-pitches (to x 475, bar y -100 to -27). (3) It turns up the right side and climbs about two-thirds of the way back toward the line (to y 155). (4) It turns left into a short top bar about 1.25 stroke-pitches long (x 294-475, y 82-155). The top bar ends free: it touches neither the downstroke nor the line. The result looks like a square-cornered hook or a one-and-a-quarter-turn rectangular spiral under the line. Glyph advance 589.
letters.note: The font form is measured exactly. 'Medium' because the medieval forms of this sign vary, and it was not checked here whether the font follows a particular manuscript. The name is uillenn 'elbow, angle', which suits the angled shape.
letters.medievalTreeGloss: edlenn, honeysuckle [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]

letters.name: ifín (later pín)
letters.form: BELOW the line, a lattice of four straight oblique strokes hanging from the stemline down to B-stroke depth. Two strokes run down to the right ('\') and two run down to the left ('/'). The two strokes running down to the right go from the line at x about 75 and 230 down to about 370 and 530. The two running down to the left go from the line at about 360 and 515 down to about 60 and 220. The strokes cross at four points arranged in a diamond: left and right crossings at mid-depth (x about 215 and 375, y about 98), one near the top centre (x 295, y about 198) and one near the bottom centre (x 295, y about 0). This leaves a small diamond-shaped cell in the middle. The effect is two X's interlaced side by side, a doubled ébad hung beneath the line. Glyph advance 589.
letters.note: The font form is measured. Manuscript forms vary and were not checked here. The later name pín and the value p belong to the medieval tradition, after the letter p entered Irish through loanwords [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication].
letters.medievalTreeGloss: pine or gooseberry (glosses vary) [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]

letters.name: emancholl
letters.translit: ae; also used for x / ch
letters.form: ABOVE the line, a grid standing on the stemline. Four parallel upright strokes rise from the line at the H-group pitch (x 114-187, 258-331, 402-475, 546-619) to y 961. That is about 1.7 times the height of an ordinary H-stroke, which reaches 695. Four horizontal crossbars cross them at even intervals (y 385-458, 529-602, 673-746, 817-890). Each bar runs from x 43 to 690, so it projects 71 units beyond the outer uprights on each side. Between the line and the top bar this makes a grid of 4 rows x 3 columns of square cells, each 71 units. The uprights stick up 71 units above the top bar. Glyph advance 733.
letters.note: The name means 'twin of coll (C)', and the four uprights are coll's four strokes, doubled by the crossbars. The font form is measured; whether it follows a particular manuscript was not checked.
letters.medievalTreeGloss: witch-hazel in modern summaries [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]

letters.name: peith (peithboc)
letters.form: A second horizontal bar lying BELOW and parallel to the stemline, detached from it, with a gap of 35 units (bar y 173-246). It is as thick as a stroke (73 units) and shorter than the line: it starts 94 units in and stops about 128 units before the line ends (x 94-495 of 623). There are no upright strokes. It looks like an equals sign whose lower bar is shorter. Glyph advance 589.
letters.note: A late scholastic sign for p, a sound the original alphabet lacked. Unicode encodes it separately from ifín/pín. The name peithboc is usually explained as 'soft b' [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]. The font form is measured; its manuscript basis was not checked.
letters.aicme: supplementary (not one of the five forfeda)

marks.form: A bare stretch of stemline (x 0-479, y 281-314), with no strokes.
marks.note: Unicode general category Zs, a space separator, checked in this session. It is the word divider in Ogham text, and it is drawn VISIBLY as stemline. In JavaScript, String.prototype.trim() removes it and /\s/ matches it (both tested in this session with Node). Python's re \s also matches it. A transliterator that trims input or splits on \s will silently destroy Ogham word spaces.

marks.form: A '>' chevron of two straight strokes. They start at full height above and full depth below at the left edge (x 0), and converge to the right on the line at about x 230-294. From that point the stemline begins and runs right (to x 489). It reads like the fletching of an arrow at the start of the line.
marks.note: Opens a text. General category Ps (opening punctuation), checked in this session.

marks.form: The mirror image: the stemline comes in from the left and ends at the point of a '<' chevron, whose two arms open to the right (to x 455).
marks.note: Closes a text. General category Pe (closing punctuation), checked in this session.

lettersSource: The 20 feda in the stone and manuscript order (B L F S N / H D T C Q / M G NG Z R / A O U E I), the five forfeda (EA OI UI IA AE) and peith (P). Names are given in Old Irish forms as in McManus (1991), remembered. Values are given for stones and for manuscripts. Characters, code points and Unicode names come from the Ogham block U+1680-U+169F, checked in this session against UCD 14.0. FORMS are measured stroke by stroke from the glyph outlines of Noto Sans Ogham 2.001 (@fontsource/noto-sans-ogham 5.3.0), outlines measured in this session, horizontal manuscript layout. The page should SET Ogham in this font (ogham subset U+1680-169C; woff2 3,896 bytes, woff 1,960 bytes; SIL OFL 1.1), not draw it. The forms let an illustrator check or reproduce the font and draw a stone-style vertical version. Stone convention: the arris (edge) of the stone is the stemline, read upward (usually up the left edge, sometimes over the top and down). B-group strokes go on one face (to the right), H-group on the other (to the left), M-group across the edge obliquely, vowels as notches on the edge. Medieval manuscript forms of the forfeda vary, and were not compared with the font in this session. Numeric is null: ogham letters carry no numerical values in the tradition. Geometry measured from Noto Sans Ogham 2.001 (@fontsource/noto-sans-ogham 5.3.0), outlines measured in this session, 1000 units/em, horizontal (manuscript) layout read left to right: the stemline is a straight horizontal bar 33 units thick (y 281-314). Each stroke is a straight bar 73 units thick. Strokes of the first two groups are 381 units long. Strokes of a letter are evenly spaced at a pitch of 144 units. The first stroke starts 114 units after the start of the line, and the line runs on 148 units past the last stroke. Glyphs overlap their neighbours by 34 units, so the stemline runs unbroken through a word. All outlines are straight segments: no curves, no ring-ends.

secretOghams.count: nearly a hundred named varieties; counts of about 92-100 are given depending on how sub-varieties are reckoned [from memory: no web search was possible in this session; verify before publication]
secretOghams.principle: Most are either (a) acrostic word-lists, where each letter is replaced by a word beginning with it from one class (birds, colours, crafts, kings, rivers, saints...), or (b) graphic variants: changed stroke shapes, positions, doublings or diagrams. A few are bodily (hand, shin, nose).

treeLayers.layer: 1. Original letter names (Primitive Irish, c. 4th-6th c.)
treeLayers.what: A mix of tree names (birch, alder, willow, oak, hazel; perhaps pine and ash) and ordinary words (fear, ingot, field, sulphur, earth...). Meanings are partly uncertain.

treeLayers.layer: 2. Medieval learned doctrine (Auraicept, In Lebor Ogaim; texts of c. 7th-14th c.)
treeLayers.what: Every letter is explained as a tree, sometimes by forced glosses (úath = whitethorn, tinne = holly, gort = ivy). Ogham is "climbed as a tree is climbed". Trees are graded in classes, as in Old Irish law.
treeLayers.source: Calder 1917; Kelly 1976 on the legal tree-list

treeLayers.what: Beth-Luis-Nion order, a 13-month tree calendar with fixed dates, a goddess-cult reading, and divination and "tree astrology". These are not found in any medieval source.

transliterator.notes: Match "ng" before "n". Forfeda digraphs should be an option, off by default, because the stones do not use them. Show modern equivalences for j, y, w, v, k, x and p as conventions, not historical spellings. Never trim() or split on \s (it eats U+1680). For a stone-style display, rotate the horizontal line 90 degrees anticlockwise so that it reads bottom to top.

links.relation: Ogham was built on Latin grammatical analysis, and the Welsh stones pair it with Latin capitals.
Lucian's Ogmios (Heracles 1) in the debate over the name. Macalister's abandoned theory of a Greek-alphabet origin.
Both are northern epigraphic scripts with learned medieval name-poems (rune poems / Bríatharogam). A runic origin for ogham is a minority view.
Cipher comparison: Carney's cipher thesis and the Ogam Tract's substitution oghams against Trithemius's polygraphy.
Same encoding principle: a letter named by group and position in a grid (aicme x number of strokes).
The Auraicept sets Irish and ogham in a Babel frame beside Hebrew, Greek and Latin.

cautions: NO WEB SEARCH WAS POSSIBLE in this session (the shared search budget was exhausted before this item ran). Everything except the Unicode data and the font measurements is from memory and must be verified before publication.
Keep the three layers apart on the page: original names, medieval tree doctrine, and Graves's modern calendar (treeLayers).
Do not print the Graves tree-calendar dates as tradition. If shown, label them "Graves 1948 / modern".
Do not print a Book of Ballymote folio or a Calder page until checked (ISOS digitisation; Calder 1917). None is given here.
Bríatharogam wordings and their paraphrases are from memory. Check each against Calder 1917 and McManus 1988 before printing.
The bird- and colour-ogham lists are partial and from memory.
The forfeda forms are measured from Noto Sans Ogham. Manuscripts draw the forfeda differently, so do not caption the font forms as "the Book of Ballymote forms".
U+1680 OGHAM SPACE MARK is whitespace (Zs): JavaScript trim() strips it and \s matches it (tested). The transliterator and any validator must allow for this.
Unicode letter names use Modern Irish spellings (BEITH, NION, CEIRT, NGEADAL, EADHADH...); the page text should use Old Irish names and give Unicode names only as labels.
Ogham is not in Agrippa. Do not present it as one of his alphabets.
Do not reproduce the emblems or texts of living Druid or Pagan organisations that use ogham.
Mount Callan and other antiquarian "finds" are cautionary tales about forged ogham. Never present an inscription without its corpus number.
